clue.text: Hard work's not good outside

indicators.note: the clue says hard work is not good, so the letter for good is taken away

parts.note: a grind is a long stretch of hard, tedious work

explanation.surface: A grumble that strenuous labour is no good once you are outside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' removes G from GRIND. The definition is a noun: the outer skin of fruit or cheese.
explanation.definitionFit: Rind is the tough outer layer of a fruit or cheese, its exterior covering.

clue.text: Shakespearean heroine, one blocking most of entry

indicators.note: the numeral stands in the way, sitting inside the shortened word for entry
only most of the word for entry is used, so its final letter is dropped

parts.note: a portal is a doorway or grand entrance
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A heroine of the stage plants herself across a doorway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'most of' trims PORTAL to PORTA; 'blocking' puts I inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: She is the clever lawyer-in-disguise of The Merchant of Venice, a leading female role in the Bard's plays.

clue.text: Hard on detective seizing bishop over English source of sting

indicators.note: in a down clue, over means placed above the next piece

parts.note: H is the pencil abbreviation for hard
taken as written

indicators.note: the detective grabs hold of the bishop, so that letter sits within

parts.note: a private eye is a detective
B is the chess notation for bishop

explanation.surface: A tough sleuth arrests a cleric, and an English stinger turns up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'seizing' puts B inside EYE to make EYBE; 'over' sets that above E in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A worker bee carries a barbed stinger and is a familiar cause of painful stings.

clue.text: Cross, upset, in part of playground entrance

indicators.note: the turned word sits inside the playground equipment

parts.note: swings are a standard piece of playground equipment

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means turned upside down, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a rood is a crucifix, a cross

explanation.surface: Someone angry and upset at a school gate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' suits a down entry: the cross is turned upside down, making DOOR, and 'in' sets it among the playground's swings.
explanation.definitionFit: Doors on hinges that open both ways form a common entry to kitchens and saloons.

clue.text: Inmate? Row if a person is free before end of year

indicators.note: letters set free are released from their order and rearranged
only the final letter of the word year is used

explanation.surface: A prison row over whether someone is to be released before the year is out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is free' rearranges ROW IF A PERSON; 'end of' gives R from 'year'. The question mark marks the definition as an example: a captured soldier is one kind of inmate.
explanation.definitionFit: A captured combatant held in a camp is a kind of detainee, an inmate of sorts.

clue.text: Annoyance caused by an albatross?

parts.note: the Ancient Mariner had to wear the dead albatross hung about his neck, so the bird literally hurt there, and the phrase for that hurt is also slang for any nuisance

explanation.surface: What a large seabird does to irritate you.
explanation.walkthrough: In Coleridge's Rime of the Ancient Mariner, the sailor wears the albatross he shot round his neck.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a tiresome person or thing that irritates, an everyday nuisance.

clue.text: Ribald and sincere? That's initially misplaced

indicators.note: that word's first letter is put out of place, moved further along within the word for sincere

parts.note: a hearty welcome is warm and sincere

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether bawdy and heartfelt go together, and decides it was out of place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That's' points back to the word for sincere: its initial H is 'misplaced', moved from the front of HEARTY to after the T. 'and' joins the two halves.
explanation.definitionFit: Earthy humour is coarse and crude, as bawdy and lewd jokes are.

clue.text: Cheer band that's wrecked farm completely

parts.note: to root for a team is to cheer it on, in American usage

indicators.note: the band is smashed up, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: a ranch is a large farm

explanation.surface: Fans cheer a band whose gig trashed a farm.
explanation.walkthrough: Root is American for cheer on a team. 'wrecked' scrambles the band to AND B, which sits between cheer and farm.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means thoroughly, down to the roots and every branch, wholly and radically.

clue.text: Frenchman embracing evening's companion in city flat

indicators.note: the Frenchman hugs his partner, so that word sits inside his name

parts.note: Pierre is a typical French man's name
a date is the person you spend a romantic evening with

explanation.surface: A French man hugs his partner for the night in his apartment in town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'embracing' wraps the Frenchman round his date; the answer is French for 'foot on the ground'.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase names a small second home kept in town for occasional stays.

clue.text: Absence of agreement in corner

parts.note: no as in 'no money' means an absence of something
OK is a word of agreement

explanation.surface: A disagreement in some quiet corner.
explanation.definitionFit: A small recess or secluded spot is a cosy corner.

clue.text: Garden feature unexpectedly bad in origin

indicators.note: the letters turn up in an unexpected arrangement

parts.note: birth is where something has its origin

explanation.surface: A garden ornament that turns out to have come from a bad start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unexpectedly' rearranges BAD with BIRTH, the word 'origin' supplies.
explanation.definitionFit: A shallow basin where birds wash is a typical ornament in a garden.

clue.text: Be a letdown: hamfistedly assist with first of furniture in home improvement?

indicators.note: the jumbled letters and the extra letter go inside the abbreviation

parts.note: DIY, do-it-yourself, is home improvement done by the owner

indicators.note: done clumsily, so the letters are jumbled
only the opening letter of the word furniture is used

explanation.surface: A clumsy helper with the furniture spoils a home makeover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hamfistedly' scrambles the helper's word to SSATIS, 'first of' takes F from furniture, and 'in' puts both within do-it-yourself.
explanation.definitionFit: To fail to satisfy someone is to disappoint, to leave them unhappy.

clue.text: Uproar when bottom gets hit

parts.note: a riverbed is the bottom of a river
to lam is to beat or thrash

explanation.surface: A row breaks out when someone is smacked on the backside.
explanation.definitionFit: A scene of wild noise and chaos, named after the old London madhouse.

clue.text: Dutch explorer's charm left one uninvolved

indicators.note: the two letters play no part, so they are removed from the word for charm

parts.note: a talisman is a lucky charm
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A Dutch seafarer's lucky amulet left someone unmoved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uninvolved' removes L and I from TALISMAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Abel Tasman was the 17th-century Dutch navigator who reached Tasmania and New Zealand.

clue.text: Mountain custom ignoring one in favour of European characters

parts.note: an alp is a high mountain

indicators.note: with ignoring, this tells us one letter is dropped and another taken instead

parts.note: a habit is a custom or practice
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A Swiss practice is set aside in favour of European ways.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ignoring ... in favour of' swaps the I of HABIT for E, giving HABET.
explanation.definitionFit: The full set of letters used to write a language is its set of written symbols.

clue.text: Silver medallist is back

definitions.meaning: the runner-up who takes silver comes in behind the winner
to back a motion at a meeting is to support it formally

explanation.surface: The runner-up in a race is back again.
explanation.definitionFit: A runner-up finishes in the place after first; to support a proposal is to endorse it at a meeting.

clue.text: Composer's skill held in reserve, nothing less

indicators.note: the skill is kept inside the shortened word
the word for reserve is short of its letter for nothing

parts.note: to book a table is to reserve it
O is the round symbol for nothing, zero
art is skill, as in the art of cooking

explanation.surface: A composer's talent kept back without anything else.
explanation.walkthrough: Reserve is the verb, as in reserving a table; 'less' takes the zero out to give BOK, and 'held in' tucks skill inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Béla Bartók was a twentieth-century Hungarian composer.

clue.text: Current measure after last month's escape

indicators.note: the measure comes after the month

parts.note: December is the last month of the year, abbreviated DEC
an amp, ampere, measures electric current

explanation.surface: An electrician reports a reading taken at the end of December.
explanation.definitionFit: To decamp is to leave suddenly or secretly, to flee or run off.

clue.text: Theatre role (not lead) is attempt to show skill

indicators.note: the leading letter of the role is dropped

parts.note: a part is a role in a play
a try is an attempt

explanation.surface: An actor's bit part, not the lead, is a chance to show talent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not lead' cuts PART to ART; 'lead' sounds like the starring role but means the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Artistry is creative talent or craftsmanship, a skilled ability.

clue.text: Examination covering book about clans?

indicators.note: the test wraps round the letter for book

parts.note: a trial is a test or examination

explanation.surface: A test that includes a book about family groups.
explanation.walkthrough: 'covering' puts B inside TRIAL. The definition is an adjective phrase: tribal means relating to clans or tribes.
explanation.definitionFit: Tribal describes what relates to a tribe or kin group, the social unit of a clan.

clue.text: Food store that's partly sidelined

indicators.note: only part of the word sidelined is used, a run of letters within it

explanation.surface: A grocery shop that has been partly pushed aside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'partly' points to the letters inside 'siDELIned'.
explanation.definitionFit: A delicatessen is a shop selling prepared foods, cheeses and cooked meats.

clue.text: Severe chap behind reorganisation of trains

indicators.note: the man stands behind, after the rearranged letters
the word trains is reorganised into a new order

parts.note: a gent is a chap, a gentleman

explanation.surface: A stern man is behind the shake-up of the rail timetable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reorganisation of' scrambles the railway word to ASTRIN, and 'behind' sets the chap after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Astringent criticism is harsh and biting, as a severe review is.

clue.text: Point is to get stuck into G&T

indicators.note: the word is pushed into the drink's letters, stuck inside them

parts.note: G&T is gin and tonic, read here as its two letters
taken as written

explanation.surface: The aim is to tuck into a gin and tonic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'get stuck into' places IS between G and T. The phrase also means to set about eagerly, which is the surface sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The gist is the main point or essence of what is said.

clue.text: The cake and flask (brewed) that may be seen around fine coffee party?

indicators.note: the mixed letters go round the letter for fine
like coffee made in a pot, the letters are mixed up

parts.note: F is the pencil abbreviation for fine

explanation.surface: Cake and a flask of fresh brew are laid out at a gathering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brewed' rearranges THE CAKE with FLASK; 'around' puts that round F. The question mark warns that the definition is in English but the answer is German.
explanation.definitionFit: The German word names an informal social gathering over coffee and cake.
